name: Brow tint kit
lead: A brow tint kit is a product containing a semi-permanent dye and an oxidizing developer that colours eyebrow hairs, and usually the skin beneath them, for several weeks. It is used to make pale, sparse or greying brows look darker, denser and more defined without daily pencil or powder. Tints are offered as a salon or brow-bar service and as home kits. [1]

The kits are inexpensive and the effect is temporary. The main safety literature concerns contact allergy to hair-dye ingredients, particularly para-phenylenediamine (PPD) and related compounds, with case reports describing dermatitis and eye inflammation after eyelash and eyebrow dyeing. No controlled trials of home brow tint kits were identified. [2][3][4]

Eyebrows matter in appearance partly because they are mobile and visible: Wikipedia notes that recent research points to communication, including conveying recognition and sympathy, as their primary function [5]. People who tint their brows are working with that feature by increasing contrast between brow hair and skin, so that shape and expression read more clearly.
infobox: No color additives approved for dyeing eyebrows or eyelashes [6]

paras: A typical kit includes a tint cream or gel, a developer, a mixing dish and an applicator, with a barrier cream to limit skin staining. Professional and home procedures generally start with a patch test and cleansing, followed by application of the dye for a few minutes and removal with a damp pad. [1]

Reference sources describe results as lasting around three to six weeks on the hair, with skin staining fading sooner, depending on hair type, aftercare and product. Brands named in these sources include RefectoCil and Godefroy. [1]

Darkening the brows with pigments is long-standing: ancient Egyptians are described as using kohl, and henna and turmeric pastes are described in other cultures. Chemical tints are reported to have emerged in the early 20th century, and professional brow-tint services became widespread in salons from about the 1980s. [1] Social media trends such as the no-makeup look are said to have increased interest more recently. [1]

Brow fashion has changed repeatedly. Wikipedia records hikimayu in Japan from the eighth century, in which brows were shaved and painted higher on the forehead, the removal of brows by some high-status Elizabethan women, the return of thin plucked brows in the 1920s and 1930s, and shaved brow lines among some young people in the 1990s and 2000s [5].

The dye deposits colour in the hair shaft and temporarily stains the skin. Oxidative hair dyes commonly rely on aromatic amines such as PPD, which are the main sensitizers described in the allergy literature. [3]

Wikipedia lists alternatives and companions to tinting: brow pencils, gels, powders and shadows for temporary fullness, cosmetic tattooing (microblading) that implants pigment in small cuts, and eyebrow transplants that move follicles from the scalp [5]. Grokipedia says tinting is often paired with brow lamination and shaping in salons [1].

The product changes colour contrast on the hairs, making sparse or pale brows look more defined; this is described in reference works but has not been measured in controlled studies. The colour fades as dye wears off and hairs shed. [1]

A 2017 review of PPD allergy describes the compound as a frequent cause of allergic contact dermatitis and discusses diagnosis and management. [3] Case reports describe allergic dermatitis and periorbital swelling after permanent eyelash dye, and blepharoconjunctivitis from chloro-PPD contact allergy after eyelash colouring. [2][4]

Product instructions and clinicians commonly advise a patch test before use and caution that dye must not reach the eye. Home use has been described as carrying more risk of uneven results and staining than professional application. [1]

The US FDA states that coal-tar hair dyes are not permitted for dyeing eyelashes or eyebrows, that no color additives are approved for dyeing eyebrows or eyelashes, and that product caution statements warn that use in the eye area may cause blindness. The agency advises a skin test before each use, because reactions can develop over time, and names PPD as a common cause of allergic reactions. FDA also says it has no reliable evidence linking today's coal-tar hair dyes to cancer [6]. Plant- and mineral-based colourants such as henna are described as approved for hair colour use [6].

Some brow-tint products are marketed in the US as eyebrow products despite this position, and in other jurisdictions, such as the EU, cosmetic ingredient rules are set separately. Salon practitioners generally position professional application as lower risk than home use [1].

Tinting is discussed as a low-cost way to make light brows read as fuller, and the site rates the effect as strong but temporary. It is often paired with brow lamination or shaping in salon menus. [1]
No studies found that test brow tint kits for appearance outcomes. The related literature consists of case reports and reviews on allergic reactions to eyelash and hair dyes. [2][3][4]

Grokipedia describes brow tinting as having surged with the no-makeup makeup and clean girl trends, with social media amplifying its visibility, and as a quick add-on in salons [1]. For people with fair or greying brows, it is described as a way to avoid daily brow makeup [1]. On forums where grooming is discussed, tinting is mentioned as a low-cost step for sparse light brows.

timeline.event: Chemical tints reported to emerge as an alternative to kohl and henna. [1]
Dedicated professional brow-tint formulas spread in salons. [1]

angle.text: A tint kit raises the contrast of the brows against the face, which makes light or thin brows look fuller and easier to frame. The effect lasts until the dye fades, usually a few weeks.
